patient.chief_complaint: Progressive behavioral change, new seizures, and involuntary facial movements for 16 days
patient.history_present_illness: A 27-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman was brought to the emergency department by her boyfriend who reports a 16-day history of alarming and progressive neurological deterioration. The illness began with approximately 5 days of flu-like symptoms including fever (maximum 38.6), headache, and fatigue that resolved spontaneously, followed by a clear interval of 3-4 days during which she appeared well. Approximately 12 days ago she began developing behavioral changes: initial insomnia and irritability progressed to frank paranoia with the belief that her boyfriend was being 'controlled by outside forces.' She told her mother that she was seeing shadowy figures in the periphery of her vision. She was brought to an urgent care clinic 9 days ago and given a diagnosis of drug-induced psychosis, which the boyfriend disputes vigorously given her absence of substance use confirmed on drug screen. Over the following week she developed increasingly prominent facial movement abnormalities that her boyfriend describes as uncontrollable grimacing, repetitive lip movements, and jaw-clenching. She had two convulsive episodes: the first lasted about one minute and occurred at home 5 days ago, and the second, lasting two minutes, prompted this ED visit today. After today's seizure she was confused, combative, and her blood pressure was 162/98 (baseline typically 110/70). Her temperature post-seizure is 38.2. Her boyfriend specifically asks the team 'Could this be that anti-NMDA encephalitis I read about online?'

neurological_exam.mental_status: Severely confused and agitated. Not oriented. Unable to follow commands consistently. Continuous orofacial dyskinesias — lip-smacking, jaw-clenching, tongue-thrusting. Periodic echolalic repetition of examiner's last few words. Post-ictal slowing at onset of exam, improving over 30 minutes.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4mm bilaterally, reactive. Continuous involuntary perioral and jaw movements. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.motor: Distal choreoathetosis of upper extremities, bilaterally. Strength grossly preserved on brief exam.
neurological_exam.additional: Autonomic instability: HR 128, BP 162/98, diaphoresis. Temp 38.2. No meningismus.

findings.frequency: 1-2 Hz delta with superimposed 25-40 Hz beta
findings.morphology: Extreme delta brush pattern — rhythmic delta waves (1–2 Hz) with superimposed fast beta activity (25–40 Hz) producing a characteristic brush-like appearance.
One electrographic seizure captured during recording, lasting 80 seconds

eeg.impression: Severely abnormal EEG. One electrographic seizure captured. Clinical correlation recommended.

mri.impression: Subtle bilateral frontal subcortical changes. No enhancement or diffusion restriction. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential_by_imaging.rationale: Bilateral medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensities with frontal subcortical signal changes; imaging pattern consistent with autoimmune limbic involvement
Less likely — bilateral symmetric temporal involvement without unilateral predilection or hemorrhagic change
No structural correlate on MRI to account for signal changes; clinical correlation required

differential.key_features: Viral prodrome, fever, CSF pleocytosis — but HSV PCR negative, bilateral temporal changes, EDB pathognomonic
Behavioral change — but drug screen negative, orofacial dyskinesias not typical of substance psychosis

optimal_actions.action: LP with anti-NMDAR antibodies and full CSF panel

critical_actions: EDB on EEG is pathognomonic — begin immunotherapy immediately
Pelvic imaging identifies large teratoma — urgent surgical referral
SIADH with Na 126 requires careful management — fluid restriction and electrolyte monitoring
contraindicated_actions: Attributing symptoms to drug-induced psychosis given negative drug screen
Rapid sodium correction — risk of osmotic demyelination
Delaying immunotherapy for antibody confirmation when EDB is present
key_reasoning_points: Complete classic triad: viral prodrome → psychiatric symptoms → seizures → orofacial dyskinesias → autonomic instability in a young woman
Extreme delta brush on EEG is pathognomonic — allows clinical diagnosis even before antibody confirmation
Very high antibody titer (serum 1:640) reflects severe disease
Large teratoma (4.5 cm) must be resected urgently
Severe SIADH (Na 126) requires careful electrolyte management

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Classic straightforward anti-NMDAR encephalitis with viral prodrome, complete triad, extreme delta brush on EEG, high-titer antibodies, and large left ovarian teratoma.
